summary: Malaysia's WFH fuel-crisis policy is showing early positive signals in mobility reduction, but long-term effectiveness depends on private sector participation and structural PT investment. The MF-Index at 58 reflects a meaningful departure from pre-crisis normal without reaching lockdown-level suppression.

signals.detail: Public sector WFH delivering ~29M litres/week — 40% of MCO peak savings at a fraction of the economic cost. Extending to private professional sector could double this figure within 30 days.
Ridership projected to fall 8–12% as commuter trips decline. This eases Prasarana overcrowding during peak hours but creates revenue pressure that may slow PT investment.
Unlike MCO, retail, logistics, and manufacturing continue at near-full mobility. 2020–2022 precedent shows minimal GDP impact from 40% WFH in the services sector.
WFH mandate exclusively benefits urban office workers. Logistics drivers, factory workers, and field staff — who travel furthest and spend proportionally more on fuel — receive no relief.
Extended WFH risks eroding PT ridership habits. Workers breaking their daily commute rhythm may default to private car travel when the mandate ends, reversing hard-won modal shift gains.

recommendation: Extend WFH to private professional sector via corporate tax incentive (50% deduction on remote-work infrastructure) to double fuel savings to ~58M L/week. Simultaneously accelerate MRT3 Circle Line to lock in PT habits before WFH ends. Target MF-Index below 50 within 60 days.
